prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping lets many neutral atoms be interrogated at once, bringing optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged after the full first-round exchange: B053 for Katori and Ye, as a single-part prize. What the exchange sharpened is what the citation must say. The new element is the magic-wavelength lattice, which removes the light shift of the clock transition so that very many atoms can be held tightly and interrogated at once; that is a different invention from controlling a single ion and a different one from the frequency comb, and it is what delivers the stability that made accuracy near 1e-18 reachable. The result is reproduced at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, and it has produced physics beyond timekeeping: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres and bounds on drifting constants. Four members prefer it and the other four name it as an alternative, so no other candidate is acceptable to the whole committee in this way. I no longer treat the redefinition of the second as part of the case, since Johansson is right that it is a metrological milestone and not a scientific one. The credit also fits the three-name limit with room to spare: Katori for the proposal and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for the accuracy, stability and many-body clock regime.
statement.case_against: The objection I cannot dismiss is the one the chair put as the first question: whether a precision-measurement invention built on the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize has the standing of a new window on nature (B009) or a closed fundamental question (B046). It is a judgement about what the prize should honour, and a committee that weights discovery above invention could reasonably rank B053 lower. A second reservation is that two names leave out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the later SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, and the supplied credit cannot settle the relative weight of Katori's proposal and Ye's programme. Finally, I am an atomic theorist and my field proximity may make me too ready to admire precision spectroscopy; the committee should discount my first place accordingly.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the 2016 prize did not cover the quantum spin Hall prediction, Z2 classification or the HgTe observation, so B013 is not overlapped in the way the clock is by the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and that clean credit is not a measure of scientific consequence.
responses.response: I accept the first part. The 2016 citation was about topological phase transitions and topological phases in the Kosterlitz-Thouless-Haldane line, and the Kane-Mele and HgTe results are different discoveries, so I no longer count 2016 as a disqualifying overlap and I keep B013 as my first alternative. I do not accept that the comb and ion prizes overlap the lattice clock more closely: they honoured the comb and the control of a single ion, neither of which solves the problem of interrogating many neutral atoms without a light-shift penalty. That is why the citation must be written around the lattice scheme. On clean credit I agree it is not a measure of consequence, but it is a precondition for a prize, and B013 still cannot be allocated: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe system that Molenkamp measured, Hasan's three-dimensional work is a separate strand, and no trio covers them. If you can tell me how a citation for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would handle that omission without misdescribing the history, I will weigh B013 more heavily; so far the draft does not.

responses.point: Pearce keeps IceCube (B009) as his first alternative, argues that a clock prize does not recognise a new window on nature, and asks the committee to argue explicitly whether metrology counts as discovery; he also asks that the B053 citation not overreach into ion-clock territory.
responses.response: I agree on the drafting and have changed my own citation to say what the lattice adds, namely magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, so that it does not claim ion-clock accuracy milestones. On discovery against invention, the statutes name both, and the lattice clock is an invention whose consequences were measured, not merely claimed. But I do not think the answer settles B009. The diffuse flux is secure and a new window is the strongest kind of case, so I would take B009 seriously in a later year. The obstacle this year is the one you and others have noted: the credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is representative, AMANDA and Baikal contributions are outside it, and source identification is still at 3 to 5 sigma. I would not move B009 above B053 unless the committee can state a defensible three-name allocation, and the first-round exchange has not produced one.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first, sees no maturity question, and says he would not resist B053 if the Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee allocation cannot be made defensible; he concedes Della Negra is as defensible a CMS founder as Virdee.
responses.response: The scientific case for B046 is the strongest on the list and I do not weigh it against the clock on merit. The question the chair asked was whether a defensible trio exists, and your own file says it does not: Virdee against Della Negra on the CMS side, and on the ATLAS side a choice between Gianotti, as spokesperson at the time of the announcement, and Jenni, as the founding spokesperson, which a leadership-based credit cannot decide on scientific contribution. A prize that must say in its citation that three names stand for two collaborations of thousands is weaker than one with a credit that maps onto the achievement. If you or another member can put forward a trio whose roles are verified and defensible, I would move B046 up from outside my alternatives; I have not listed it because the allocation remains unresolved.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that eight years of independent replication make B033 mature enough, that the flat-band prediction and correlated phases are stable, and that a precise instrument lineage is a different standard from one that rewards a new physical regime; he would accept B053 ahead on timing.
responses.response: I accept that the flat-band prediction and the existence of correlated phases at the predicted angle are reproduced, and I have kept B033 as my second alternative for that reason. My objection is narrower than maturity in general. The credit is what the discovery rests on, and the experimental discovery is credited to a group leader while Cao, who carried out the decisive measurements, cannot be named. Pairing remains unsettled, which matters because the citation would otherwise have to describe the superconductivity. I think the lattice clock also rewards a new regime, not only an instrument lineage: many-atom interrogation at 1e-18 with controlled many-body shifts is a regime that did not exist. I am glad you would accept B053 ahead on timing, and I would not oppose revisiting B033 once the pairing question is better settled.

responses.point: Kroll holds that discovery against invention is not a useful dividing line, that the ion-clock overlap is separable because the lattice solves a different problem, and that the citation should keep both Katori's and Ye's contributions visible.
responses.response: I agree with the separability argument and with keeping both names visible, and the revised citation does this by describing the scheme in the first clause and its precision realisation in the second. I would still not write that the separation is clean without qualification, and I would not let it rest on discovery against invention being a false dichotomy: some members will weigh it, and the citation should be defensible to those who do. Where I would correct the record is on the credit: Katori's proposal is not only the idea and Ye's work not only the execution. Ye's group's Fermi-degenerate clocks and many-body shift control are part of what the lattice clock became, which is the reason I would not draft the citation around Katori's proposal alone or around accuracy alone.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a precision-measurement invention as equal in standing to a discovery-type result, which is a judgement of purpose that the scientific evidence cannot settle.

How the relative weight of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's accuracy and many-body programme should be expressed in a citation; the supplied credit pairs them but does not settle the relative contribution.
I have not independently verified the latest published clock uncertainties and comparison figures, and I rely on recollection of priority dates.
Whether a defensible three-name allocation exists for B046 or B009; if one does, my ranking of them against B053 could change.
The contributions of uncredited groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, and the strontium and ytterbium groups) cannot be added within the supplied credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B053: my profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and none with other clock groups named in this discussion. I work in atomic theory and have an extended collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, plus collaborations with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich; none of these involve the credited names on the shortlist, but my proximity to atomic and optical physics remains a possible source of bias towards B053 and I keep it disclosed. Nothing in the round-1 exchange changes this disclosure.
